parts.label: (a)
parts.part_stem:
The variation of stress with strain for a metal P is shown in Fig. 3.1.

{{figure:figure_3_1}}

Fig. 3.1

Point E is the elastic limit of the metal.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Use Fig. 3.1 to determine the Young modulus for P.

markscheme_points.text: E = σ / ε or E = gradient

hints: Hint 1: Focus on the first straight section of the graph in Fig. 3.1 where stress is directly proportional to strain. Pick a clear point on that straight line to read off values.
Hint 2: Remember to convert strain from percent to a decimal fraction, then divide the stress value by the strain value to get the gradient.
parts.proper_answer: Using $E = \text{stress} / \text{strain}$ in the linear region, e.g. $12 \times 10^{7} \text{ Pa} / 0.0050 = 2.4 \times 10^{10} \text{ Pa}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall What Young Modulus Means on This Graph**
For a metal below its limit of proportionality, stress and strain follow Hooke's law. That means $E$ is just the steepness of the straight line at the start: $$E = \frac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}}$$ So you do not need force and extension separately, the axes already give you stress and strain.

Step 2: **Read a Point and Fix the Units**
Choose a point well up the straight line to reduce reading error. For example at strain $0.50\%$ the stress is about $12 \times 10^{7} \text{ Pa}$. Convert percent to a pure number: $$0.50\% = 0.0050$$ Then calculate: $$E = \frac{12 \times 10^{7}}{0.0050} = 2.4 \times 10^{10} \text{ Pa}$$ Any other point on the straight line gives the same result within reading tolerance.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: State the conditions necessary for an object to be in equilibrium.

markscheme_points.text: resultant force (in any direction) is zero
resultant moment / torque (about any point) is zero

hints: Hint 1: Think separately about what would make an object start to move in a straight line, and what would make it start to spin.
Hint 2: For full equilibrium both types of motion must be prevented, so consider the total force and the total turning effect about any point.
parts.proper_answer: The resultant force on the object is zero and the resultant moment about any point is zero.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **No Overall Push**
If the vector sum of all forces is not zero, the object must accelerate in the direction of the resultant force by Newton's second law. So for equilibrium: $$\text{resultant force} = 0$$ This keeps the centre of mass at rest or moving at constant velocity.

Step 2: **No Overall Turn**
Even with zero net force, a pair of equal opposite forces can still spin an object. To prevent angular acceleration the turning effects must also cancel: $$\text{resultant moment about any point} = 0$$ Both conditions together give complete equilibrium with no linear or rotational acceleration.

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem:
A wire is used to hold a uniform shelf AB horizontally in equilibrium as shown in Fig. 3.2.

{{figure:figure_3_2}}

Fig. 3.2 (not to scale)

The wire is connected to the midpoint of shelf AB at an angle of $50^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. The shelf is attached to a wall by a hinge at A. The length of shelf AB is $0.65\text{m}$ and its weight is $33\text{N}$.
A cup of weight $1.5\text{N}$ rests on the shelf with its centre of gravity at a horizontal distance of $0.12\text{m}$ from B.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: By taking moments about A, determine the tension in the wire.

markscheme_points.text: sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments 33 × (0.65 / 2) + 1.5 × (0.65 − 0.12) = T sin 50° × (0.65 / 2)

hints: Hint 1: Taking moments about A is clever because the hinge forces at A then have no moment. Identify the two clockwise weights and their distances from A.
Hint 2: Only the vertical part of the wire tension provides an anticlockwise moment about A. Think how to get that vertical component from the $50^{\circ}$ angle and the distance to the midpoint.
Hint 3: Set total clockwise moment equal to total anticlockwise moment and solve for $T$.
parts.proper_answer: Clockwise moments: $33 \times 0.325 + 1.5 \times 0.53$. Anticlockwise: $T \sin 50^{\circ} \times 0.325$. Equating gives $T = 46 \text{ N}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **List the Clockwise Moments About A**
The uniform shelf acts at its centre, $0.65/2 = 0.325 \text{ m}$ from A. The cup is $0.65 - 0.12 = 0.53 \text{ m}$ from A. Both weights try to rotate the shelf clockwise about A: $$M_{shelf} = 33 \times 0.325$$ $$M_{cup} = 1.5 \times 0.53$$

Step 2: **Write the Anticlockwise Moment From the Wire**
The wire pulls at the midpoint, $0.325 \text{ m}$ from A, at $50^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. Only the component at right angles to the shelf counts for moments: $$T_{vertical} = T \sin 50^{\circ}$$ So: $$M_{wire} = T \sin 50^{\circ} \times 0.325$$ anticlockwise.

Step 3: **Apply Balance of Moments and Solve**
In equilibrium clockwise equals anticlockwise: $$33 \times 0.325 + 1.5 \times 0.53 = T \sin 50^{\circ} \times 0.325$$ $$11.52 = T \times 0.249$$ $$T = 46 \text{ N}$$ to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text:
The stress in the wire is $1.5 \times 10^{7}\text{Pa}$.

Determine the radius of the wire.
hints: Hint 1: You know the pulling force in the wire from the last part and the stress it produces. Think how stress links force to the thickness of the wire.
Hint 2: Once you have the cross-sectional area, use the circle area formula to work back to the radius.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the Area From Stress**
Stress is force per unit area: $$\sigma = \frac{F}{A}$$ Rearrange for area: $$A = \frac{F}{\sigma} = \frac{46}{1.5 \times 10^{7}} = 3.07 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^{2}$$

Step 2: **Convert Area to Radius**
For a circular wire $A = \pi r^{2}$, so: $$r = \sqrt{\frac{A}{\pi}} = \sqrt{\frac{3.07 \times 10^{-6}}{\pi}}$$ $$r = 9.9 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$$ That is just under $1 \text{ mm}$, which is sensible for a supporting wire.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text:
More items are added to the shelf, doubling the stress in the wire. The wire is made of the metal P from (a).

Use Fig. 3.1 to state and explain whether the wire will behave plastically or elastically as the stress doubles.

markscheme_points.text: elastic limit is not reached or (new) stress is less than (stress at) elastic limit or (new) strain is less than (strain at) elastic limit

hints: Hint 1: Start by working out the new doubled stress value and compare it by eye with the stress at point E in Fig. 3.1.
Hint 2: Recall what it means to stay below the elastic limit in terms of whether the deformation is reversible.
parts.proper_answer: Doubled stress $= 3.0 \times 10^{7} \text{ Pa}$ is still well below the elastic limit at E ($\approx 26 \times 10^{7} \text{ Pa}$), so the wire behaves elastically and returns to original length.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Compare the New Stress With the Elastic Limit**
Doubling gives: $$1.5 \times 10^{7} \times 2 = 3.0 \times 10^{7} \text{ Pa}$$ Look at Fig. 3.1. Point E, the elastic limit, is at about $26 \times 10^{7} \text{ Pa}$. The new stress is almost ten times smaller, so the elastic limit is not reached.

Step 2: **Decide Elastic or Plastic**
Below the elastic limit the atomic bonds are only stretched, not permanently slipped. The wire still obeys elastic behaviour and will return to its original length when unloaded, not show plastic permanent deformation.
